## Summary

The episode warns that higher rates and complex AI financing may expose balance-sheet risks. Eisman distinguishes visible Nvidia vendor financing from Meta's unconsolidated venture, but his interpretation of EY's audit work contradicts the procedures he reads aloud. He also considers agentic commerce, streaming competition and a qualified correction to his earlier short-against-the-box discussion. The rate threshold and market-correction timing are not tightly defined enough for a clean forecast score.

Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.

<a id="youtube-vKLPLywZcp0-c016"></a>
### 016. He corrects his short-against-the-box suggestion by invoking the year-end closing and subsequent 60-day holding exception to constructive-sale treatment.

**Mixed** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | supporting

[Source at 25:02-26:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vKLPLywZcp0&t=1502s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The cited exception exists, but it additionally requires unreduced risk of loss throughout the 60 days. The original discussion omitted constructive sales and this correction does not fully spell out that third condition.

Qualification: He describes his own timing hedge and directs listeners to specialist advice; the planned reopening is in 2027.

Assessment test: Apply all statutory conditions to an actual position; distinguish reduced price exposure from automatic tax deferral.

- [Publication 550 (2025): Constructive Sales](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p550) (2025 tax-year edition, inspected 2026-11-10): Shorting the same appreciated stock generally creates a taxable constructive sale. The closed-transaction exception requires close by 30 days after tax-year-end, 60 days continued ownership and no reduction of risk during those 60 days.
